data.title: High energy prices cost India an extra ₹6-7 trn annually: Tarun Kapoor
data.description:
India's high oil and gas import dependence, coupled with high global energy prices, is costing the country between ₹6 lakh crore and ₹7 lakh crore extra annually, and the solution lies in citizens cutting avoidable fuel consumption, Tarun Kapoor, adviser to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in the Prime Minister's Office (PMO), said today.
 
Speaking at a Confederation of Indian Industry (CII) event on energy security, he said the impact of this large dependence on imports is being felt across the economy, including in fuel prices, freight rates, and overall inflation.
 
"Large dependence on imports has shown that we are so vulnerable that we may be caught in a tight situation and it can be disastrous for the country. Just this high price of crude and natural gas is costing us at least ₹6-7 lakh crore extra every year," Kapoor said.
 
 
India imported over 293 million tonnes (MT) of crude oil and petroleum products last financial year (2025-26) at a cost of over ₹13 lakh crore, according to Petroleum Planning and Analysis Cell (PPAC) data. In the first seven months of the current financial year, the country spent ₹11.4 lakh crore to import 161 MT of crude oil and products.
 
"The government has so far absorbed quite a bit of the increase in price which should have been passed on to the customers. The oil companies have very graciously absorbed a part of that increase but had it all been passed on to the consumers, as has been done in most of the countries like US or Europe, the impact on all consumer goods and supplies would have been disastrous," Kapoor said.
 
He added that countries like China have been able to overcome the shock by building huge energy storage capacity, but that solution has its limits, as storage capacity cannot be built for two-three years.
 
"Storage can be built at best for 90 days or a little more but that also helps because if even a part of your requirement comes from what your stored, you at least know when to buy or play with the market. We are like a person who goes every day to the market to buy his ration and comes back and eats it. This is because we have very little storage," Kapoor said.
 
He also said that given the huge energy consumption of the country, strategies like diversification of oil supplies, looking for alternative sources, and entering into long-term contracts, too, have limited gains. He said it is more important that citizens cut avoidable consumption, reiterating Prime Minister Narendra Modi's recent call.
 
Modi had recently urged citizens to cut fuel, gold, and foreign-linked consumption to conserve foreign exchange reserves and ease import pressures amid the West Asia and Strait of Hormuz crisis.
 
"Citizens can do that. What we have seen is that initially when the PM gave the call, there was a bit of a reduction but the economy is growing," Kapoor said, adding that the last few months have witnessed a more-than-normal increase in energy consumption due to economic growth.
 
He added that the country needs dedicated policy intervention to ramp up the pace of the shift towards electric trucks, a cost-effective mode of transport.

data.title: Britannia Industries CMO Puneet Das quits within 10 months of joining
data.description:
Leading bakery foods company Britannia Industries on Friday said its Chief Marketing Officer, Puneet Das, has resigned to pursue an opportunity outside the organisation, according to a regulatory filing.

Das, who joined Britannia in February 2026, will be relieved from the company's services with effect from the close of business on December 9, 2026, according to a regulatory filing.

"Puneet Das, Chief Marketing Officer, has decided to pursue an opportunity outside Britannia and has resigned from the services of the Company," said Britannia.

Das was appointed Chief Marketing Officer of Britannia Industries effective February 16, 2026. His exit comes less than 10 months after taking charge of the marketing function at the biscuit and bakery major.

data.title: Pet insurance explained: What is covered and why claims may get rejected
data.description:
Pet insurance can help owners manage the cost of unexpected veterinary treatment, including hospitalisation, surgery, diagnostic tests and medicines. But paying a premium does not mean every veterinary bill will be reimbursed. Waiting periods, pre-existing conditions, treatment-specific caps, co-payments and exclusions can significantly reduce the payout.
 
The actual value of a pet insurance policy depends not just on the sum insured but also on how much of a particular treatment the insurer agrees to cover.
 

What does pet insurance cover?

 
Pet insurance policies in India can cover expenses arising from illnesses and accidents, including veterinary consultations, diagnostic tests, prescribed medicines, hospitalisation and surgeries. Depending on the insurer and the policy selected, coverage may extend to outpatient department (OPD) treatment, dental care, specialised therapies, emergency ambulance services and third-party liability.
 
 
Ashwini Dubey, business head – home and pet insurance at Policybazaar, said some policies also offer benefits such as pet boarding, teleconsultations, death or loss benefits, trip cancellation, behavioural treatment and eligible pregnancy complications. However, these benefits may require separate covers or add-ons.
 
The extent of coverage can make a difference when an unexpected medical emergency arises.
 
Dubey shared three claim examples. In one case, a pet suffering from blood in the urine and stomach discomfort underwent investigations and kidney stone surgery, for which the insurer paid ₹42,991. In another, an accidental fall led to Grade 2 medial patellar luxation (MPL), requiring orthopaedic surgery, with a claim payout of ₹59,237.
 
In a third case, a pet swallowed a finger ring and required medical intervention, resulting in a claim payout of ₹35,390.
 
Arti Mulik, chief technical officer at Universal Sompo General Insurance, said hospitalisation expenses can range from ₹1,000 to ₹50,000, depending on the severity of the condition, while surgeries could cost even more.
 

What is not covered, and why can claims be rejected?

 
Pet insurance is designed to protect against unforeseen expenses rather than existing illnesses or predictable routine costs.
 
Mulik said common exclusions include pre-existing illnesses, cosmetic procedures, treatment by unqualified persons, conditions arising from deliberate neglect and government-banned breeds. Routine check-ups and vaccinations may be covered under specific plans or add-ons. Most policies also have waiting periods of 30 to 90 days, depending on the product.
 
Girish Sehgal, chief – health underwriting, claims, customer service and operations at ICICI Lombard, said the insurer's Paw Care policy generally excludes pre-existing conditions, subject to applicable continuity provisions. Claims arising during the initial 30-day waiting period are also excluded, except those resulting from accidents.
 
Routine expenses such as vaccinations, grooming, bathing and nail clipping are not covered under the general policy terms. Certain claims may also become inadmissible if prescribed preventive medicines or vaccinations have not been taken.
 
Owners should also check whether OPD treatment is covered, as consultations, diagnostic tests and medicines may not qualify under the base policy.
 

Why may the sum insured not be enough?

 
A policy offering ₹1 lakh in cover does not necessarily reimburse ₹1 lakh for every treatment. Treatment-specific sub-limits, deductibles and co-payments can reduce the payout.
 
Dubey illustrated this with an example of a minor illness claim under HDFC ERGO's Make Your Own Plan, which is capped at 25 per cent of the applicable illness sum insured or ₹15,000, whichever is lower. If the illness sum insured is ₹40,000, the maximum payout under this limit would be ₹10,000, even if the veterinary bill is ₹40,000.
 
Mulik said the premium should not be the sole criterion for buying insurance. Consider two owners who insure similar dogs for ₹25,000. One policy has no co-payment and higher surgery limits, while another offers a lower premium but imposes a 20 per cent co-payment and a surgery cap of ₹10,000.
 
For a ₹15,000 surgery, the second policy could pay less than ₹10,000 because of its sub-limit, despite the owner having paid premiums regularly.
 

What should pet owners check before buying insurance?

 
Sehgal advised pet owners to examine the sum insured, treatment-specific sub-limits, deductibles, co-payments, waiting periods, exclusions and age- and breed-based eligibility.
 
Dubey said owners should also check renewal conditions, premium revisions, claim-intimation timelines, cashless veterinary hospital availability, pre-authorisation requirements and claim-processing timelines.
 
Before purchasing, owners should disclose the pet's medical history, check vaccination requirements and understand whether coverage can continue as the pet ages.
 
While filing a claim, they should notify the insurer within the prescribed timeline, retain prescriptions, diagnosis reports and itemised bills, and ensure the pet's identification matches the policy.
 
Pet insurance is a financial protection tool against unexpected medical expenses, not a guarantee that every veterinary bill will be paid. Reading the policy wording before purchasing can help owners avoid unpleasant surprises when their pet needs treatment.

data.title: Vivo X500 Pro Max first impressions: Premium phone built around photography
data.description:
The Vivo X500 Pro Max is not a smartphone that blends into the crowd. From its large circular camera module to its sizeable display, the device makes its intentions clear. It is designed for users who place photography high on their list of priorities, and Vivo has gone a step further by offering optional teleconverter attachments to extend its imaging capabilities. Having spent some time with the device, its design, in-hand feel and display have made a good first impression.
 
Starting with the design, the Vivo X500 Pro Max retains the circular camera arrangement seen on its predecessor. However, the company has made some changes to the rear panel. The upper portion of the glass back, which houses the camera module, is slightly raised and slopes gently into the rest of the panel. This gives the phone a distinctive appearance without making the camera housing feel like an entirely separate component.
 
 
The aluminium frame adds to the construction, while the glass back has a smooth finish with a subtle pattern. It does attract fingerprints, though. The phone is available in Apex Orange and Eternal Black colour options, with different finishes on the rear panel.
ALSO READ: Vivo X500 series launched in India: Check specs, price details, and more
Despite its sizeable camera hardware, the X500 Pro Max measures between 7.95mm and 8.12mm in thickness, depending on the colour variant, and weighs 225g or 229g. It is not a lightweight smartphone, but the weight distribution makes it reasonably comfortable to hold. The index finger naturally rests below the camera module, which also helps when holding the phone in landscape orientation for photography. However, its large footprint means two-handed operation is often more convenient.
 
The camera system is where Vivo wants the X500 Pro Max to distinguish itself. The phone features a 50MP primary camera, a 50MP ultra-wide camera and a 200MP ZEISS APO telephoto camera. The latter has an 85mm equivalent focal length and is the centrepiece of the setup.
 
Vivo is also offering optional teleconverter attachments to extend the phone's photography capabilities. The range includes a 200mm equivalent ZEISS Telephoto Extender Gen 2 and a 400mm equivalent Gen 2 Ultra. There is also an Imaging Grip Kit with a physical shutter button and zoom dial. Together, these accessories make the phone resemble a compact camera setup and are aimed at users interested in wildlife and long-distance photography.
 
Moving to the front, the X500 Pro Max features a 6.85-inch 2K ZEISS Master Color AMOLED display with a 144Hz refresh rate. The panel has narrow, symmetrical bezels and a flat design, while a small punch-hole houses the front camera. The screen looks sharp, with deep blacks and vibrant colours.
ALSO READ: GTA 6 India launch: First impressions, prices, editions and download size
The LTPO panel can dynamically switch its refresh rate between 1Hz and 144Hz, depending on the content. Vivo claims peak brightness of up to 5,000 nits, while the high-brightness mode is rated at 2,000 nits. The display also supports Dolby Vision and HDR10+, while an ultrasonic fingerprint sensor is embedded underneath.
 
The Vivo X500 Pro Max makes a good first impression with its design, in-hand feel and AMOLED display. The teleconverter attachments also give it a different proposition from conventional flagship smartphones. However, their usefulness and the extent to which they improve the photography experience need closer examination.
 
There is still more to assess, including camera performance across different conditions, processing capabilities, software and battery life. The full review of the Vivo X500 Pro Max will be out soon.

Vivo X500 Pro Max: Price and availability

The smartphone is available for pre-booking in India, with open sales scheduled to begin on December 3.
  • 12GB RAM + 256GB storage: Rs 164,999
  • 12GB RAM + 512GB storage: Rs 179,999
Accessories available for separate purchase:
  • 400 mm Equivalent vivo ZEISS Telephoto Extender Gen 2 Ultra: Rs 27,999
  • 200 mm Equivalent vivo ZEISS Telephoto Extender Gen 2: Rs 15,999
  • Imaging Grip Kit: Rs 11,999
  • Phone Strap: Rs 2,699
  • Magnetic Case: Rs 1,499 (X500 Pro Max and X500 Pro)
Customers can also get the 12GB RAM + 512GB storage variant of the Vivo X500 Pro Max with the Photography Kit at Rs 229,999. It includes the smartphone, a 200mm equivalent ZEISS Telephoto Extender Gen 2, a 400mm equivalent ZEISS Telephoto Extender Gen 2 Ultra and a shoulder strap.

data.title: Sebi aims to cut FPI onboarding time to five business days: Chairman
data.description:
Markets regulator Sebi is aiming to reduce the onboarding time for Foreign Portfolio Investors (FPIs) from several months to as little as five business days through digital workflows and system integration, its chairman Tuhin Kanta Pandey said on Friday.

Addressing the 17th Capital Markets Conference organised by ASSOCHAM, Pandey said the regulator has also proposed removing the additional disclosure framework for FPIs, bringing India's regulatory framework closer to global standards.

"Through digital workflows and system integration, we aim to cut FPI onboarding from months to as little as five business days," Pandey said.

Over the past few months, Sebi has taken several measures to ease the compliance burden for FPIs.

 

Under the SWAGAT-FI (Single Window Automatic and Generalised Access for Trusted Foreign Investors) initiative, around 740 FPIs, accounting for nearly 17 per cent of FPI assets under custody, have registered.

"SWAGAT-FI gives trusted, low-risk FPIs single-window access, simpler compliance and longer KYC review cycles," he added.

On the regulatory front, Pandey said Sebi is undertaking a comprehensive review of the Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements (LODR) framework to eliminate duplicative disclosures in filings with the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (MCA). The regulator also plans to replace multiple stock exchange fines for the same compliance lapse with a single penalty.

Sebi is simultaneously reviewing the Issue of Capital and Disclosure Requirements (ICDR) framework, which governs initial public offerings (IPOs), follow-on public offerings (FPOs), preferential issues and qualified institutional placements (QIPs). The review will also cover the SME IPO framework and the Innovators Growth Platform.

For stock brokers, the regulator is exploring a graded compliance framework under which regulatory obligations would be aligned with a broker's scale, client exposure and dependence on technology.

Pandey said the Securities and Exchange Board of India (Sebi) is also working towards harmonising the regulatory frameworks governing Investment Advisers and Mutual Fund Distributors.

On the technology front, the regulator is exploring the development of a domestically governed artificial intelligence (AI) model for the securities market, enabling smaller regulated entities to access secure and affordable AI solutions. Guidelines on the responsible use of AI are being prepared, while a proposed AI sandbox will allow innovators to test applications in a controlled environment, he said.

In the corporate bond market, Sebi is developing a market-making framework in consultation with the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Ministry of Finance, focusing on liquidity, market infrastructure and access to repo facilities. Fixed Income Channel Partners will help expand bond distribution via regulated online platforms, while Phase II of Demat 2.0 will enable secondary-market trading in tokenised bonds.

In the cash market, the regulator is reviewing the framework for short selling and securities lending and borrowing (SLB) to improve liquidity and price discovery. For Alternative Investment Funds (AIFs), the regulator is simplifying requirements linked to investor consent, related-party transactions, co-investments and exits.

In the case of Real Estate Investment Trusts (REITs) and Infrastructure Investment Trusts (InvITs), Sebi aims to reduce the listing timeline from six working days to three days and simplify the process for rights issues.

Highlighting the growth of India's capital markets, Pandey said companies raised around Rs 9 lakh crore through equity and debt in the first seven months of the current financial year. So far, 235 IPOs have collectively raised approximately Rs 1.45 lakh crore, while more than Rs 5 lakh crore has been mobilised through corporate bonds.

data.title: Vivo X500 series launched in India: Check specs, price details, and more
data.description:
Vivo has launched its X500 series smartphones in India, introducing three models: the X500, X500 Pro and X500 Pro Max. The new flagship line-up, co-engineered with ZEISS, puts the focus on photography and videography, with features such as telephoto autofocus tracking. The X500 Pro Max leads the range with a 200MP ZEISS APO telephoto camera and support for an optional 400mm equivalent teleconverter.
 
All three smartphones run Android 17-based OriginOS 7 and are powered by MediaTek Dimensity 9600-series chipsets. While the X500 Pro Max and X500 Pro use the Dimensity 9600 Pro, the standard X500 is powered by the Dimensity 9600M.

Vivo X500 Pro

As part of the launch offers, buyers can avail up to 10 per cent cashback on eligible bank cards and UPI transactions, or a 10 per cent upgrade and exchange bonus. data.title: Canada Express Entry: 600 invited for PR in first STEM draw since 2024
data.description:
Canada on Thursday resumed category-based Express Entry draws for science, technology, engineering and mathematics (STEM) occupations after a gap of more than 31 months, issuing 600 invitations to apply (ITAs) for permanent residency.
 
Immigration, Refugees and Citizenship Canada (IRCC) set the minimum Comprehensive Ranking System (CRS) score at 547 for the draw. Candidates needed eligible work experience in one of 11 occupations to qualify.
 
This was the third Express Entry draw in November. It followed a Provincial Nominee Program draw on November 23, which issued 1,999 invitations, and a Canadian Experience Class (CEC) draw earlier in the month.
 
How does Canada's Express Entry system work?
  
Express Entry is Canada's online system for managing applications for permanent residence under three federal economic immigration programmes:
 
Federal Skilled Worker Program
Federal Skilled Trades Program
Canadian Experience Class
 
Candidates create an online profile and receive a CRS score based on factors such as age, education, work experience and language proficiency. IRCC conducts regular draws and invites candidates who meet the applicable score and category requirements to apply for permanent residence.
 
Details of the November 26 STEM draw
 
The November 26 draw was conducted at 12:52 UTC. Its key details were:
 
Draw type: Category-based selection – STEM occupations
Invitations issued: 600
Minimum CRS score: 547
Rank required: 600 or higher
Tie-breaking date: December 2, 2025, at 16:52:51 UTC
 
The tie-breaking rule applies to candidates with the minimum CRS score of 547. Those who submitted their Express Entry profiles before the specified date and time were given priority over candidates with the same score who submitted their profiles later.
 
Why is this STEM draw important?
 
IRCC had not conducted a STEM-specific Express Entry draw since April 11, 2024, when it issued 4,500 invitations with a minimum CRS score of 491.
 
Earlier STEM draws included:
 
December 2023: 5,900 invitations, with a CRS cutoff of 481.
July 2023: 500 invitations, with a CRS cutoff of 486.
 
The November 26 draw differs from these earlier rounds in three ways.
 
First, its CRS cutoff of 547 is considerably higher than the previous STEM draw thresholds. Second, the number of invitations has fallen to 600, compared with thousands in the 2023 and 2024 rounds.
 
Third, the eligible occupation list has been reduced from 24 NOC codes to 11 under the revised Express Entry categories announced in February 2026.
 
Which 11 occupations qualify for the STEM draw?
 
The following occupations under Canada's National Occupational Classification (NOC) 2021 system were eligible for the November 26 selection round:
 
1. Architecture and science managers (TEER 0)
2. Cybersecurity specialists (TEER 1)
3. Civil engineers (TEER 1)
4. Mechanical engineers (TEER 1)
5. Electrical and electronics engineers (TEER 1)
6. Industrial and manufacturing engineers (TEER 1)
7. Geological engineers (TEER 1)
8. Civil engineering technologists and technicians (TEER 2)
9. Mechanical engineering technologists and technicians (TEER 2)
10. Electrical and electronics engineering technologists and technicians (TEER 2)
11. Insurance agents and brokers (TEER 3)
 
Several technology occupations, including software developers (NOC 21232), software engineers (NOC 21231), data scientists (NOC 21211) and web developers (NOC 21234), are no longer included in the revised list.
 
What are the eligibility requirements for STEM candidates?
 
Under the 2026 category-based selection framework, candidates must have at least 12 months of cumulative work experience in an eligible occupation within the previous three years.
 
The experience can be acquired in Canada or abroad and does not need to be continuous. It must meet IRCC's requirements for full-time work or its equivalent in part-time employment.
 
This is a change from the previous six-month work experience requirement and narrows the pool of candidates eligible for STEM-specific draws.
 
What should candidates do after receiving an ITA?
 
Candidates invited in the November 26 draw have 60 days from the date of invitation to submit a complete application for permanent residence.
 
They should:
 
1. Check their eligibility: Verify that their work experience matches one of the 11 eligible NOC occupations. Job duties, rather than job titles alone, determine the appropriate NOC classification.
2. Prepare supporting documents: These include valid language test results, an Educational Credential Assessment (ECA), employment reference letters, police clearance certificates and medical examination documents, as applicable.
3. Meet the deadline: Submit the complete permanent residence application within 60 days of receiving the ITA. Failure to meet the deadline means the invitation expires.
4. Update relevant information: Disclose changes in employment, education, language scores or other circumstances that could affect CRS scores or eligibility.
 
An invitation to apply does not guarantee permanent residence. IRCC assesses the supporting documents and verifies that applicants meet the programme's eligibility requirements before making a final decision.

data.title: Power sector needs ₹200 trillion investment by 2047: Minister Manohar Lal
data.description:
India’s power sector would require an investment of around ₹200 lakh crore by 2047, to be mobilised through public sector company listings and private investment under the public-private partnership (PPP) model, said Union Power Minister Manohar Lal at the Power Ministers’ Conference on Friday.
 
He also highlighted the need to address power evacuation constraints, expand energy storage, and strengthen regional resource adequacy planning to integrate renewable energy and meet rising demand from data centres, electric vehicles, and industries.
 
Considering the increasing demand, he suggested that industries move to a three-shift system for even distribution of power. He stressed the necessity for states to implement smart meter installations and adopt prepaid smart meters, especially for government offices.
  
The minister also urged state governments to ensure timely payment of electricity bills by government departments, suggesting that provisions for these payments be made in advance in the annual budget.
 
Distribution companies (discoms) had total outstanding borrowings of ₹7.26 lakh crore as of March 31, 2025, even as they posted a combined profit of over ₹2,600 crore. The minister said there is a need to ensure the financial viability of discoms.
 
On nuclear power, Lal said that eight sites are ready for inspection, while 25-30 sites have been offered for development. States would need to identify more locations to expand nuclear power generation, he said, adding that nuclear energy would play a critical role in meeting rising round-the-clock power demand from data centres and artificial intelligence.
 
Power Secretary Pankaj Agarwal, also present at the event, said that around 60 gigawatts (GW) of capacity was added in the past 12 months, with 87 per cent of the addition coming from non-fossil sources.
 
Commenting on the rising demand, he also said that India's per capita consumption has risen from 957 kilowatt-hours in 2013-14 to 1,488 kilowatt-hours in 2025-26. "This year also showed us where the system is under strain. In October, 2026, while power was surplus during the solar hours, there were days when we could barely meet the demand during the evening peak," the secretary added.
 
A weak monsoon, high temperatures, and irrigation load pushed demand up by 12 per cent to 39 per cent in several states, including Karnataka, Gujarat, Madhya Pradesh, and Maharashtra, Agarwal noted.

data.title: Nomura raises December RBI rate hike call to 50 bps, BoB sticks to 25 bps
data.description:
Nomura on Friday raised its expectation for the Reserve Bank of India's (RBI's) December policy rate hike to 50 basis points (bps) from 25 bps earlier, citing a sharper-than-expected rise in food prices. Bank of Baroda (BoB), however, continues to expect a 25 bps hike when the Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) announces its decision on December 4.
 
Nomura expects the repo rate to rise to 6 per cent. It sees a 60 per cent probability of a 50 bps hike, with a 5-1 vote split, and a 40 per cent chance of a 25 bps hike, which is the consensus expectation. Its base case is a 50 bps hike, with the stance remaining at "calibrated tightening".
 
 
BoB said a rate hike was a given, but the extent of the increase remained uncertain. It expects the MPC to opt for a 25 bps hike, citing an improvement in the geopolitical situation after the US midterm elections.
 
Nomura said its daily food price trackers had recorded some of the sharpest monthly increases in the past couple of years, driven by sticky components such as cereals and pulses. It expects Consumer Price Index (CPI)-based inflation to rise to around 6.4 per cent in November from 6.1 per cent in October. This would take the average inflation for the October-December quarter to 6.3 per cent, against the RBI's forecast of 6 per cent.
 
The brokerage expects headline inflation to remain above 6 per cent for at least two quarters, compared with the RBI's earlier projection of one quarter. Core inflation momentum has also picked up as companies pass on higher input costs, it said.
 
On growth, Nomura expects gross domestic product (GDP) data due on November 30 to show growth of over 7.5 per cent, against the RBI's forecast of 7.2 per cent. It expects the central bank to raise its FY27 GDP growth forecast by 40 bps to around 7.5 per cent and its CPI inflation forecast by 10 bps to 5.3 per cent. The core inflation forecast is likely to remain unchanged at 4.4 per cent.
 
Nomura said the RBI's guidance on the timing of the rate hike would be important in determining the next policy move. If the central bank presents the increase as front-loaded, the likelihood of another 25 bps hike in February would be lower. However, if it is seen as a catch-up move, a February hike would remain possible.
 
Its base case is for the RBI to pause at 6 per cent, although there is a risk of another 25 bps hike in February or April. Basing monetary policy decisions on headline inflation rather than core inflation could risk overtightening, it added.
 
BoB said inflation remained a concern, with October CPI inflation at 6.1 per cent, food and beverages inflation at 8.5 per cent, and core inflation at 4.5 per cent. Reservoir levels were lower at 61.6 per cent as of November 19, while rabi sowing of wheat, pulses, and oilseeds had also been lower so far.
 
It expects inflation to remain in line with the RBI's forecasts of 6 per cent for the third quarter and 5.7 per cent for the fourth quarter. The share of goods and services recording inflation above 4 per cent rose sharply in October, pointing to a broadening of price pressures, it said.
 
BoB expects GDP growth of 7.4 per cent in the second quarter and 7.2 per cent for the full financial year, with an upward bias. It expects another 25 bps hike in February and possibly one more in April, depending on inflation trends. This would take the terminal repo rate to 6.25 per cent, giving a real return of around 1 per cent, with inflation remaining above 5 per cent for the year.
 
Both Nomura and BoB expect the RBI to address tight liquidity conditions. Nomura said the central bank could restore the minimum daily cash reserve ratio (CRR) maintenance requirement to 90 per cent from 99 per cent and signal forex buy-sell swaps.
 
BoB said liquidity remained delicately placed, with the RBI relying on variable rate repo (VRR) auctions. Faster credit growth than deposit growth, liquidity absorption following the FCNR(B) deposit mobilisation scheme, the higher CRR maintenance requirement, and elevated government cash balances were among the factors weighing on liquidity, it said.
 
The bank expects the RBI to undertake open market operation (OMO) purchases and forex swaps, under which it buys dollars from banks. Such operations would also help check the rupee's appreciation, it said.
 
The rupee has strengthened to around ₹92.50 per dollar from ₹94.87 at the beginning of November, BoB said. Foreign portfolio investors (FPIs) have invested $16.4 billion in November, while Brent crude has averaged $93.5 per barrel in the 16 days since the US elections, compared with $120.2 per barrel in the preceding 16 days.
 
The 10-year government bond yield has remained in the 7.20-7.25 per cent range in recent sessions, suggesting that the market has priced in a 25 bps rate hike, BoB said. Yields had been moving towards 7.50 per cent before the US elections.
 
The US 10-year Treasury yield has cooled to 4.85-4.90 per cent, while the Federal Reserve is expected to raise rates at least twice more by 25 bps each, it said.
 
Nomura said the market was pricing in only a 25 bps hike and would be hawkishly surprised by a 50 bps increase. The brokerage has raised its conviction on its March 2027 one-year versus five-year overnight indexed swap (OIS) flattener trade to 4/5 from 3/5. The spread is currently at minus 12 bps, with a target of minus 35 bps by February-end.

data.title: Collegium favours a 'particular section' over merit, diversity: Ex-CJI
data.description:
Former Chief Justice of India BR Gavai on Friday wrote to President Droupadi Murmu seeking her intervention in judicial appointments and transfers. He alleged that recent Collegium recommendations favour candidates from "one particular section of the society", at the expense of merit, diversity and inclusivity.
 
In a three-page letter, Gavai alleged that candidates from one section of society were being favoured for elevation to the higher judiciary, while Scheduled Castes (SCs), Scheduled Tribes (STs), Other Backward Classes (OBCs), minorities, women and other communities were being excluded.
 
"I am constrained to voice my dissent and disappointment," Gavai wrote, alleging that recent appointments and transfers were being made in disregard of diversity, inclusion and merit.
 
 
The letter was addressed to President Murmu and marked to Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal.

Gavai questions representation in higher judiciary

Gavai said a community accounting for less than 5 per cent of India's population had secured more than 40 per cent representation in the Supreme Court in the recent past.
 
He also referred to data presented by Union Law Minister Arjun Ram Meghwal in the Rajya Sabha in March 2025.
 
According to the data, of the 715 high court judges appointed since 2018, 22 belonged to the Scheduled Castes (SCs), 16 to the Scheduled Tribes (STs), 89 to the Other Backward Classes (OBCs) and 37 to minority communities. Together, these four categories accounted for 164 appointments, or around 23 per cent of the total.
 
Gavai said the representation of different sections of society had been considered during his tenure in the Collegium.
 
In the letter, he wrote: "When I was a part of the collegium and was Chief Justice of India, I always followed the principles of diversity and inclusion."
 
He added that adequate representation was ensured for SCs, STs, OBCs, minorities and women while considering candidates for elevation to the high courts and the Supreme Court.
 
However, he alleged that recent recommendations ignored these principles. "In the recent past disturbing events have unfolded, showing complete disregard for the principles of merit and inclusivity," he wrote.

Gavai questions recent transfers and appointments

The former CJI also raised concerns over the transfer of high court judges and subsequent recommendations for their elevation.
 
He referred to an instance in which a chief justice was transferred from one high court to a smaller high court and was subsequently recommended for appointment as the chief justice of a prominent high court.
 
Gavai alleged that another meritorious and hardworking chief justice was transferred to a smaller high court to accommodate the appointment.
 
He said he had been part of the Collegium that recommended the first chief justice's transfer and later headed the Collegium when the subsequent transfer recommendation was made.
 
"I am aware of the factors that prevailed at the relevant time with the collegium for recommending such an appointment/transfer. However, on account of propriety and judicial disciple I refrain from divulging these reasons," he wrote.
 
Citing another instance, Gavai alleged that a judge who had been transferred from his parent high court to another high court on punitive considerations was subsequently appointed chief justice of a large and prominent high court.
 
"In another instance, a judge was transferred from his parent high court to another high court on punitive consideration and was subsequently rewarded by appointment as chief justice of a large and a prominent high court," the letter read.

Gavai urges President to intervene

Gavai also questioned whether the Collegium's primacy in judicial appointments could place it beyond accountability.
 
Referring to Article 124(2) of the Constitution, which provides for the appointment of Supreme Court judges by the President, he argued that the President's constitutional responsibilities remained relevant to the process.
 
He said the Collegium's recommendations being treated as decisive under judicial convention did not make the body unaccountable or absolve the President of her constitutional duties.
 
Gavai also said the executive and Parliament were stakeholders in judicial appointments and transfers. He referred to instances in which the government and legislature had requested the Collegium and high courts to consider suitable candidates from marginalised communities to improve representation.
 
He urged President Murmu to intervene, as she deemed appropriate, and remind all stakeholders of their constitutional responsibilities towards ensuring equal representation in the higher judiciary.
